title: The Singular Value Decomposition
description: The SVD of any matrix, its geometry, low-rank approximation, the pseudoinverse and its uses in machine learning.
overview: Eigendecomposition applies only to square matrices, and only some of them. The singular value decomposition (SVD) applies to every matrix, rectangular or not, and reveals its structure completely: every matrix is a rotation, followed by a stretch along coordinate axes, followed by another rotation. The stretches, the singular values, say how much each direction matters.

The SVD is the most useful single factorization in applied mathematics. It computes PCA, gives the best low-rank approximation of a matrix, defines the pseudoinverse for least squares, measures the conditioning of a problem, and underlies recommender systems, text analysis, image compression and the low-rank adaptation of neural networks.
objectives: State the SVD A = UΣVᵀ, compute it for a small matrix and describe it geometrically.
Relate singular values and vectors to the eigendecomposition of AᵀA and AAᵀ and to the four fundamental subspaces.
State the Eckart–Young theorem and compute the best low-rank approximation and its error.
Define the pseudoinverse and use it for minimum-norm least squares.
Apply the SVD to PCA, matrix norms and compression.

sections.title: The singular value decomposition
body: Imagine the matrix as a machine that takes a perfectly round ball of inputs and outputs a squashed, tilted ellipse. The ellipse has a longest axis, a next longest, and so on. The SVD reads off exactly those: the lengths of the axes (the singular values), the directions of the axes in the output (the left singular vectors), and the input directions that produce them (the right singular vectors). A long axis means the matrix amplifies that direction a lot, and a very short axis means almost nothing from that direction survives. Every m × n real matrix A can be factored as

list: U is an m × m orthogonal matrix whose columns u_i are the **left singular vectors**.
V is an n × n orthogonal matrix whose columns v_i are the **right singular vectors**.
Σ is an m × n matrix, zero except for the **singular values** σ₁ ≥ σ₂ ≥ … ≥ σ_r > 0 on its diagonal, where r is the rank.

body: In terms of action on vectors: Vᵀ rotates (or reflects) the input into a new coordinate system, Σ stretches the i-th coordinate by σ_i (and discards or adds coordinates if m ≠ n), and U rotates the result into the output space. The unit sphere is mapped to an ellipsoid whose semi-axes have lengths σ_i and directions u_i. Equivalently, A maps v_i to σ_iu_i: Av_i = σ_iu_i.
Dropping the zero blocks gives the **compact SVD**, and expanding the product gives A as a sum of rank-one matrices, ordered by importance:

From the factorization, AᵀA = VΣᵀΣVᵀ and AAᵀ = UΣΣᵀUᵀ. So the right singular vectors are the eigenvectors of AᵀA, the left singular vectors are the eigenvectors of AAᵀ, and the singular values are the square roots of the eigenvalues: σ_i = √λ_i(AᵀA). This is also how the existence of the SVD is proved: AᵀA is symmetric and positive semidefinite, so it has an orthonormal eigenbasis (the spectral theorem) with non-negative eigenvalues, which define V and σ, and then u_i = Av_i/σ_i.

sections.title: The SVD and the four fundamental subspaces
body: The SVD gives orthonormal bases for all four subspaces at once (see Vector Spaces):

The rank is the number of non-zero singular values. In floating point, a singular value is never exactly zero, so the **numerical rank** counts the singular values above a tolerance (about σ₁ · max(m, n) · 10⁻¹⁶). This is the reliable way to find the rank of a data matrix.
Singular values define the important matrix norms:

eqs: the spectral norm: the largest factor by which A stretches a vector, max ‖Ax‖/‖x‖
the nuclear norm, a convex surrogate for rank used in matrix completion
the condition number of A, for the 2-norm

body: The condition number tells how much relative error in b or A can be amplified in the solution of Ax = b. A matrix with κ = 10⁸ loses about 8 of the 16 digits of double precision, and a matrix with σ_r near zero is nearly singular.

sections.title: Low-rank approximation
body: The SVD writes a matrix as a sum of simple layers, each one a rank-one matrix, ordered from most important to least. A photograph, for example, is mostly captured by the first few layers (broad shapes and lighting), while later layers add fine detail and noise. Keeping only the first k layers gives a smaller description that looks almost the same. Keep only the k largest terms of the sum A = Σσ_iu_iv_iᵀ to get the **truncated SVD**

body.key: Eckart–Young theorem. Among all matrices of rank at most k, A_k is the closest to A in both the spectral and the Frobenius norm. The errors are ‖A − A_k‖₂ = σ_{k+1} and ‖A − A_k‖_F = √(σ_{k+1}² + … + σ_r²).

body: This is why the SVD is the tool for compression and noise reduction: the discarded part is exactly the part of smallest 'energy'. It is also the proof that PCA is optimal: for a centered data matrix X, the best rank-k approximation of X is X_k, and its row space is spanned by the top k principal components.

example.title: Compression of an image
example.problem: A grayscale image is a 1000 × 1000 matrix with 10⁶ entries. How many numbers does a rank-50 approximation need, and how much of the energy ‖A‖_F² is retained if the squared singular values beyond 50 sum to 4% of the total?
example.solution: A_k needs the k singular values and the k vectors u_i (1000 numbers) and v_i (1000 numbers): 50(1000 + 1000 + 1) = 100,050 numbers, about 10% of the original. The retained energy is 96%. Photographs have rapidly decaying singular values, so a small k looks nearly identical.

example.title: Approximation error
example.problem: A has singular values 10, 4, 2, 1. Find the error of the best rank-2 approximation in the two norms.
example.solution: Spectral: σ₃ = 2. Frobenius: √(2² + 1²) = √5 = 2.236, compared with ‖A‖_F = √(100 + 16 + 4 + 1) = 11.0, so the relative error is 20%.

list: **PCA and latent semantic analysis**: a term–document matrix is approximated by a few concepts, so that similar documents get similar low-dimensional codes.
**Recommender systems**: a ratings matrix is modeled as a product of a user matrix and an item matrix (see PCA and Dimensionality Reduction in the Machine Learning book).
**Denoising**: low-rank signal plus full-rank noise; truncation removes most of the noise.

**Efficient fine-tuning of large networks (LoRA)**: instead of updating a d × k weight matrix W, learn a low-rank update ΔW = BA with B of size d × r and A of size r × k. For d = k = 4096 and r = 8, this is 8(4096 + 4096) = 65,536 parameters instead of 16.8 million, 0.39% of the original.
**Compression of trained networks** by factorizing weight matrices.

sections.title: The pseudoinverse and least squares
body: When A is not square or not invertible, the **pseudoinverse** A⁺ gives the best substitute. From the SVD, invert the non-zero singular values and leave the zeros:

body.eq: A⁺ = V Σ⁺ Uᵀ = Σ_{i=1}^{r} (1/σ_i) v_i u_iᵀ

body: The vector x̂ = A⁺b solves the least squares problem min ‖Ax − b‖, and when there are many minimizers (A has a non-trivial null space), it is the one of **minimum norm**. When A has independent columns, A⁺ = (AᵀA)⁻¹Aᵀ, the least squares solution of the earlier chapters; when A is invertible, A⁺ = A⁻¹.

example.title: A rank-one pseudoinverse
example.solution: A has rank 1: A = σuvᵀ with σ = 2 and u = v = (1, 1)/√2. Then A⁺ = (1/σ)vuᵀ = ¼[[1, 1], [1, 1]] and x = A⁺b = ¼(4, 4) = (1, 1). Among all solutions of x₁ + x₂ = 2, the point (1, 1) is the closest to the origin, i.e. has the minimum norm.

body: Solving by the SVD shows how errors enter. The least squares solution is x̂ = Σ (u_iᵀb/σ_i) v_i. Small singular values divide by tiny numbers, which amplify noise in b enormously. Two cures:

list: **Truncated SVD**: drop components with σ_i below a threshold (use a rank-k pseudoinverse).
**Ridge regression**: replace 1/σ_i by σ_i/(σ_i² + λ). This damps small singular values smoothly and equals (AᵀA + λI)⁻¹Aᵀb (see the Regularization chapter).

example.title: Noise amplification
example.problem: A has singular values 10 and 0.001. The right-hand side b has a noise component of size 0.01 along u₂. By how much does the solution change, and what does ridge with λ = 0.01 do to that component?
example.solution: The component of x̂ along v₂ changes by 0.01/0.001 = 10, a thousand times the noise. With ridge the factor σ/(σ² + λ) = 0.001/(10⁻⁶ + 0.01) ≈ 0.1, so the change is 0.01 × 0.1 = 0.001: the noise is no longer amplified.

body: In practice, library routines for least squares (`lstsq`) use the SVD or a rank-revealing QR, so they work even when X is rank deficient, unlike the explicit normal equations.

quiz.q: What are the singular values of A = [[−3, 0], [0, 2]]?
quiz.why: Singular values are square roots of the eigenvalues of AᵀA = diag(9, 4), so they are 3 and 2 and are never negative. The sign of the −3 is absorbed into U or V.

quiz.q: A is a 5 × 3 matrix. In the full SVD A = UΣVᵀ, what are the shapes of U, Σ and V?
quiz.why: U lives in the output space ℝ⁵, V in the input space ℝ³, and Σ has the same shape as A. The compact SVD would use 5 × r, r × r and 3 × r.

quiz.q: A has singular values 6 and 2. The unit circle in the input space is mapped to an ellipse. What are its semi-axes?
quiz.a: Lengths 6 and 2, pointing along u₁ and u₂
wrong: Lengths 6 and 2, pointing along v₁ and v₂
Lengths 36 and 4, pointing along u₁ and u₂
Lengths √6 and √2, pointing along u₁ and u₂
quiz.why: A maps v_i to σ_iu_i, so the image axes have length σ_i and point along the output vectors u_i. The v_i are the input directions that produce them.

quiz.q: AᵀA has eigenvalues 49, 9 and 0. What are the rank of A and its largest singular value?
quiz.why: Singular values are the square roots of the eigenvalues: 7, 3 and 0. Only two are non-zero, so the rank is 2.

quiz.q: A 2 × 2 matrix has determinant −6 and largest singular value 6. What is its other singular value?
quiz.why: The product of singular values is |det A| = 6, so σ₂ = 6/6 = 1. Singular values are non-negative; the sign of the determinant only records a reflection.

quiz.q: A is a 4 × 6 matrix of rank 3. Which singular vectors form an orthonormal basis of its null space?
quiz.why: The null space lives in ℝ⁶ and has dimension 6 − 3 = 3. It is spanned by the right singular vectors beyond the rank. The vector u₄ spans the left null space.

quiz.q: A matrix has singular values 6, 3 and 2. What is its Frobenius norm?
quiz.why: ‖A‖_F = √(36 + 9 + 4) = √49 = 7. The value 11 is the sum of the singular values, the nuclear norm.

quiz.q: A matrix has largest singular value 1000 and smallest non-zero singular value 10⁻⁷. In double precision (about 16 digits), roughly how many correct digits can a solution of Ax = b have?
quiz.why: κ = 1000/10⁻⁷ = 10¹⁰, which costs about 10 of the 16 digits, leaving about 6.

quiz.q: A 5 × 5 matrix has computed singular values 3, 1, 10⁻³, 10⁻¹⁷ and 10⁻¹⁸. What is its numerical rank?
quiz.why: The tolerance is about σ₁ · 5 · 10⁻¹⁶ ≈ 10⁻¹⁵, so the last two singular values count as zero. Counting all non-zero floating-point values would wrongly report 5.

quiz.q: A has spectral norm ‖A‖₂ = 5, and x has ‖x‖ = 3. What can be said about ‖Ax‖?
quiz.why: ‖A‖₂ = max ‖Ax‖/‖x‖, so ‖Ax‖ ≤ 5 · 3 = 15. Equality holds only when x points along the top right singular vector v₁.

quiz.q: A has singular values 9, 5, 3 and 1. What is the Frobenius-norm error of the best rank-1 approximation?
quiz.why: By Eckart–Young the error is √(5² + 3² + 1²) = √35. The value 5 is the spectral-norm error of the same approximation.

quiz.q: A has singular values 10, 5, 2 and 1. What fraction of ‖A‖_F² does the best rank-2 approximation retain?
quiz.why: The squared values are 100, 25, 4, 1, total 130, so the retained fraction is 125/130 = 96%. The value 83% (15/18) wrongly sums unsquared singular values.

quiz.q: X is a centered data matrix with one example per row, and X = UΣVᵀ. The principal component directions are
quiz.why: The columns of V are eigenvectors of XᵀX, which is proportional to the covariance matrix. The vectors u_i live in the space of examples, not features.

quiz.q: A weight update ΔW = BA is learned for a 2048 × 2048 matrix with B of size 2048 × 4 and A of size 4 × 2048. How many parameters are trained?
quiz.why: B has 2048 · 4 = 8192 entries and A has 4 · 2048 = 8192, total 16,384, about 0.4% of the 4,194,304 entries of a full update.

quiz.q: What is the pseudoinverse of A = diag(4, 0.5, 0)?
wrong: It does not exist, since A is singular
quiz.why: The pseudoinverse inverts the non-zero singular values and leaves zeros alone. It exists for every matrix, including singular ones.

quiz.q: Among all solutions of x₁ + 2x₂ = 5, which one does the pseudoinverse solution A⁺b pick?
quiz.why: All four satisfy the equation, but A⁺b is the one of smallest norm: (1, 2) has norm √5 ≈ 2.24, versus 3.16 for (3, 1) and 5 for (5, 0) and 2.5 for (0, 2.5). It is the point on the line closest to the origin.

quiz.q: A has a singular value σ = 0.1. In solving least squares, by what factor is the noise along that direction multiplied without regularization, and with ridge λ = 0.01?
quiz.why: Without ridge the factor is 1/σ = 10. Ridge uses σ/(σ² + λ) = 0.1/(0.01 + 0.01) = 5. Ridge always shrinks the factor relative to 1/σ.

summary: Every matrix factors as A = UΣVᵀ with orthogonal U, V and non-negative singular values σ₁ ≥ … ≥ σ_r > 0. Geometrically it rotates, stretches along axes and rotates again, mapping v_i to σ_iu_i.
σ_i² are the eigenvalues of AᵀA and AAᵀ. The SVD gives orthonormal bases of all four fundamental subspaces, and the rank is the number of non-zero singular values (numerical rank uses a tolerance).
Eckart–Young: the truncated SVD A_k is the best rank-k approximation, with errors σ_{k+1} (spectral) and √Σ_{i>k}σ_i² (Frobenius). This yields PCA, compression, denoising and LoRA.
The pseudoinverse A⁺ = VΣ⁺Uᵀ gives minimum-norm least squares. Truncation and ridge regularization tame small singular values.

problems.q: Find the singular values of A = [[1, 2], [2, 4]] and its rank.
problems.solution: AᵀA = [[5, 10], [10, 20]] has trace 25 and determinant 0, so its eigenvalues are 25 and 0. The singular values are 5 and 0, so the rank is 1.

problems.q: A = [[0, 2], [−3, 0]]. Find its singular values and ‖A‖₂, ‖A‖_F.
A matrix has singular values 8, 6, 3, 1, 0.5. How many are needed to retain at least 95% of the squared Frobenius norm?
problems.solution: Squares: 64, 36, 9, 1, 0.25, total 110.25. Cumulative: 64/110.25 = 58.0%; 100/110.25 = 90.7%; 109/110.25 = 98.9%. Three singular values retain 98.9%, and two only 90.7%, so k = 3.

problems.q: Compute the least-squares solution of minimum norm to Ax = b for A = [[2, 0], [0, 0]] and b = (4, 1).
problems.solution: A⁺ = [[0.5, 0], [0, 0]], so x = A⁺b = (2, 0). The second equation 0 = 1 cannot be satisfied, and x₂ is free; the minimum-norm choice is x₂ = 0.

problems.q: A weight matrix is 1024 × 1024. How many parameters does a rank-16 factorization BA have, and what fraction of the full matrix is that?
problems.solution: 16(1024 + 1024) = 32,768 parameters. The full matrix has 1,048,576, so the fraction is 3.1%.
